evaluated.name: Cash-Burn Debt Dependence
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at)), INDICATOR(NEG(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net debt issuance predicts lower returns when firms have persistent negative operating cash flow.
evaluated.reasoning: Repeated cash burn makes net borrowing more likely to reflect liquidity pressure than productive financing. The distress condition separates this interpretation from debt issuance by healthy firms funding investment.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Deficit Dividend Resilience
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(dvc, at), 3)), INDICATOR(NEG(re), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: Persistent dividends predict higher returns among firms with an accumulated retained-earnings deficit.
evaluated.reasoning: Maintaining dividends despite negative retained earnings can reveal liquidity resilience and management confidence not evident from the distressed balance sheet alone. Smoothing payouts reduces sensitivity to one-period dividend timing and emphasizes sustained financing capacity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidity-Strained Net Borrowing
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(lct, act), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net debt issuance predicts lower returns when accompanied by a severe working-capital deficit.
evaluated.reasoning: Using net rather than gross debt issuance aligns the signal with the external-financing anomaly while distinguishing borrowing from debt rollover. The rank conjunction is high only when both net borrowing and liquidity strain are elevated, without assigning most firms an identical zero score.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-Conversion Equity Dependence
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net equity issuance predicts lower returns when reported income is not supported by operating cash flow.
evaluated.reasoning: A large income-to-cash-flow gap identifies latent liquidity pressure or aggressive accruals rather than simply classifying firms as unprofitable. Equity issuance in that state can reveal opportunistic market timing or dependence on outside capital before the underlying cash weakness becomes fully priced.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-Backed Distress Deleveraging
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at)), MIN(RANK(RATIO(oancf, at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net debt retirement predicts higher returns when a firm with accumulated losses has restored operating cash generation.
evaluated.reasoning: Negative retained earnings identify legacy distress, while positive operating cash flow distinguishes a genuine turnaround from repayment funded through asset liquidation or refinancing. Requiring strong ranks in repayment, cash generation, and legacy distress targets credible balance-sheet repair without restricting the signal to the negative-book-equity tail.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Failed Maturity Refinance
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(lct, act), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Long-term debt issuance predicts lower returns when short-term debt is still increasing and the issuer has a working-capital deficit.
evaluated.reasoning: Long-term issuance is not evidence of successful refinancing if current debt continues to grow and current liabilities exceed current assets. The conjunction identifies a financing spiral, aligns the sign with the debt-issuance anomaly, and avoids interpreting gross issuance alone as favorable market access.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Debt-Demand Mismatch Spread
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(sale, 1), at)))), MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at)), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(sale, 1), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net borrowing during revenue contraction predicts lower returns, while net repayment during revenue expansion predicts higher returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests whether debt financing is aligned with operating demand rather than substituting one liquidity proxy into an archived cash-burn signal. The two-sided construction gives the high and low portfolios coherent adverse and favorable financing states instead of treating every low conjunction score as economically equivalent.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Issuance Cash-Gap Co-Acceleration
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1))), MIN(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Returns are lower when net equity issuance and the income-to-cash-flow gap increase together, and higher when both financing dependence and the cash gap recede.
evaluated.reasoning: Changes isolate transitions into external-financing dependence rather than reusing the level net-issuance anomaly or adding another known distress characteristic. The symmetric construction may improve portfolio evidence by contrasting worsening issuer events with genuine financing and cash-conversion improvements.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Earnings-Confirmed Dividend Revision
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(dvc, 1), LAG(dvc, 1)))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(ib, at), 1)))), MIN(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(dvc, 1), LAG(dvc, 1))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ib, at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Dividend cuts accompanied by earnings deterioration predict lower returns relative to dividend increases supported by earnings improvement.
evaluated.reasoning: Earnings deterioration has an unambiguous adverse interpretation and avoids the accrual-anomaly conflict created by declining working capital. evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Depleting-Cash Payout Mix
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(prstkc, ADD(prstkc, dvc))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1)))), MIN(RANK(RATIO(dvc, ADD(prstkc, dvc))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Repurchase-heavy payouts predict lower returns when cash reserves are declining, relative to dividend-heavy payouts supported by cash accumulation.
evaluated.reasoning: Payout composition tests repurchase quality without allowing low operating profitability to dominate the signal. Conditioning through total positive payouts excludes inactive non-payers rather than assigning them a mass of zero repurchases, while the two-sided comparison gives both portfolio legs a clear economic interpretation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Recovery-Funded Net Repayment
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net debt repayment predicts higher returns when operating cash flow is improving.
evaluated.reasoning: Improving cash flow makes repayment more likely to represent a sustainable turnaround than asset liquidation or loss of credit access. Using cash-flow change rather than its level reduces exposure to the generic profitability premium and avoids the dispersion compression of the prior three-way distress conjunction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unfunded Distress Dilution
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(GROWTH(csho, 1), RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Share-count growth that is large relative to net equity cash proceeds predicts lower returns for firms with accumulated losses.
evaluated.reasoning: Distressed firms may issue shares through creditor conversions, stock compensation, or deeply discounted restructuring transactions that create substantial dilution without comparable liquidity inflows. Comparing share growth with cash proceeds separates this mechanism from the standard net share issuance anomaly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Failed Distress Equity Repair
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at)), MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net equity issuance predicts lower returns when liabilities continue to rise relative to assets at firms with accumulated deficits.
evaluated.reasoning: Equity financing should improve survival prospects only if it repairs the distressed balance sheet; rising leverage after issuance indicates that financing needs remain unresolved. The liability outcome supplies a direct failed-recapitalization test rather than another profitability or cash-holdings filter.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Episodic Debt Access Risk
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(VOL(RATIO(dltis, at), 3)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(lct, che), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Volatile reliance on long-term debt issuance predicts lower returns when current obligations substantially exceed cash reserves.
evaluated.reasoning: Issuance volatility captures unstable or episodic access to debt markets rather than another version of rising short-term debt after refinancing. The continuous cash-adjusted claims measure avoids the prior three-value historical rank and identifies firms for which inconsistent financing access creates material liquidity risk.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Repurchase-Earnings Policy Gap
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(prstkc, ADD(prstkc, dvc)), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ib, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Returns are lower when the repurchase share of payouts rises relative to the firm's earnings trajectory.
evaluated.reasoning: Increasing repurchase emphasis while earnings deteriorate indicates an aggressive or poorly timed payout response, whereas reducing repurchases as earnings weaken conserves liquidity. Using changes in payout composition avoids directly reproducing the repurchase or net-share-issuance anomaly, and the positive-payout denominator excludes inactive firms rather than assigning all non-repurchasers the same score.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dividend Smoothing Under Earnings Risk
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(VOL(dvc, 3), MA(dvc, 3)))), RANK(VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Stable dividends predict higher returns when the firm's accounting earnings are unusually volatile.
evaluated.reasoning: Low dividend variability relative to the established payout level reveals financing capacity and commitment when operating outcomes are unstable. This mechanism uses payout smoothing rather than the cash-flow-minus-income accrual measure, while the mean-dividend denominator naturally limits the comparison to economically relevant dividend payers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Emergency Debt Issuance Spike
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(dltis, at), MA(RATIO(dltis, at), 3))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(lct, che), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A spike in long-term debt issuance predicts lower returns when current claims substantially exceed cash reserves.
evaluated.reasoning: The earlier issuance-volatility signal had strong portfolio alpha but no linear slope because volatility treats issuance surges and subsequent collapses identically. Focusing on the directional deviation above the firm's issuance norm identifies active emergency financing and may preserve the adverse tail while improving cross-sectional sign consistency.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liability-Reducing Noncash Dilution
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RANK(GROWTH(csho, 1)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at)))), MUL(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Share growth not matched by equity cash proceeds predicts higher returns when it reduces liabilities at firms with accumulated deficits.
evaluated.reasoning: In this setting, unexplained share growth can represent a debt-to-equity conversion that dilutes shareholders but materially lowers default risk. Differencing ranked share growth and ranked cash issuance fixes the prior unit mismatch, while the liability reduction distinguishes recovery-oriented conversions from uncompensated dilution.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Deficit Equity Funding Share
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sstk, ADD(sstk, dltis))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Reliance on equity rather than debt issuance predicts lower returns among firms with accumulated losses.
evaluated.reasoning: For deficit firms actively raising external capital, an unusually high equity share can reveal exclusion from debt markets, severe dilution, or desperation financing. The financing-mix ratio restricts comparison to capital raisers and tests funding-source choice rather than the unconditional equity-issuance level anomaly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-Rebuilding Dividend Stability
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(VOL(dvc, 3), MA(dvc, 3)))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Stable dividends predict higher returns when the firm's cash reserve is simultaneously rebuilding.
evaluated.reasoning: Cash accumulation confirms that dividend smoothing reflects genuine financing capacity rather than an unsustainable commitment maintained through earnings volatility. This replaces the extreme earnings-risk leg that likely weakened the prior long-short alpha, while the dividend-variability ratio naturally focuses the signal on established payers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidity-Funded Debt Repair
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1))), SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltr, ADD(dltr, dltis))), RANK(RATIO(dltis, ADD(dltr, dltis)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: During cash-reserve drawdowns, repayment-dominant debt activity predicts higher returns than issuance-dominant activity.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests whether firms use liquidity to reduce debt overhang rather than replenish cash while adding debt, a financing-allocation mechanism unrelated to sales growth. The debt-transaction shares restrict the comparison to active borrowers and create interpretable repayment and issuance poles under the same liquidity shock.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dual-Market Distress Funding
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MIN(dltis, sstk), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Simultaneously raising substantial debt and equity predicts lower returns when operating cash flow is weak.
evaluated.reasoning: Tapping both capital markets while internal cash generation is poor indicates unusually broad external-financing dependence, potential debt-market limits, and severe dilution risk. The matched gross-financing amount identifies dual-market funding rather than repackaging either the debt-repayment turnaround or debt-demand mismatch signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Shareholder Priority Under Liquidity Strain
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), ADD(dltr, ADD(dvc, prstkc)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(lct, act), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Prioritizing dividends and repurchases over debt repayment predicts lower returns when the firm has a working-capital deficit.
evaluated.reasoning: The allocation ratio compares shareholder distributions with creditor repayment among firms making financing outflows, rather than relying on payout levels alone. A high shareholder share under weak current coverage can deepen rollover risk and reveal poor capital-allocation discipline.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Externally Funded Distress Payout
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MIN(ADD(dvc, prstkc), ADD(dltis, sstk)), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Simultaneously raising external capital and distributing cash to shareholders predicts lower returns when operating cash flow is weak.
evaluated.reasoning: The matched amount of payouts and external financing identifies financing churn in which distressed firms raise capital while leaking cash to shareholders. This agency and liquidity mechanism differs from dual debt-and-equity dependence because it focuses on the use of proceeds rather than the breadth of funding sources.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Financing Outflow Liquidity Burden
evaluated.expression: RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltr, ADD(dvc, prstkc)), act))
evaluated.hypothesis: Large debt repayments and shareholder payouts relative to current assets predict lower returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The ratio measures the total financing cash-outflow burden that must be absorbed by near-term operating resources, rather than recombining debt and equity issuance anomalies. High values identify firms whose repayment and payout commitments can directly impair liquidity even when each outflow might be benign in isolation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Tax-Exhausted Debt Issuance
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(pi, at)), NEG(RATIO(txt, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Long-term debt issuance predicts lower returns when pretax income and current tax payments indicate little capacity to use the debt tax shield.
evaluated.reasoning: Debt issued without taxable earnings is less likely to reflect optimal tax financing and more likely to fund losses or refinance obligations. This replaces the repeatedly unsuccessful issuance-extremeness and liquidity-gap combination with a distinct tax-capacity mechanism using a continuous distress state.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Uncovered Debt Service Gap
evaluated.expression: RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(dltr, oancf), che), at))
evaluated.hypothesis: Returns are lower when debt repayments exceed the combined support from operating cash flow and existing cash reserves.
evaluated.reasoning: The construction directly measures a dollar funding gap rather than attaching another noisy confirmation rank to net debt retirement. A positive and large gap indicates that repayment likely requires refinancing, asset sales, or further liquidity contraction, reversing the favorable interpretation of cash-backed deleveraging.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity-Funded Earnings Repair
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sstk, ADD(sstk, dltis))), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(re, 1), LAG(at, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity-heavy external financing predicts higher returns when retained earnings are simultaneously recovering.
evaluated.reasoning: Equity issuance does not directly replenish retained earnings, so improvement in retained earnings provides a non-mechanical indication that operating recovery accompanies the recapitalization. Scaling the retained-earnings change by lagged assets further prevents the capital raise itself from creating an artificial improvement through the denominator.

evaluated.name: External-Funding Exit Recovery
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), at), 1))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Returns are higher when reliance on gross external financing declines as operating cash flow improves.
evaluated.reasoning: A simultaneous financing decline and cash-flow recovery identifies firms exiting a rescue-financing cycle rather than merely repaying one form of capital with another. Using changes tests a recovery transition and avoids reproducing the level external-financing anomaly that drives several archived distress signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Earnings-Backed Equity Recapitalization
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MIN(sstk, dltr), at)), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(re, 1), LAG(at, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity issuance accompanied by debt repayment predicts higher returns when retained earnings are recovering.
evaluated.reasoning: The matched financing flow identifies cash equity recapitalizations that retire creditor claims, while retained-earnings improvement confirms that operating performance is also repairing the balance sheet. Because equity issuance does not directly increase retained earnings, the recovery leg is not mechanically generated by the financing transaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accelerating Rescue Financing
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(ACCEL(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), at))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accelerating reliance on debt and equity issuance predicts lower returns among firms with accumulated losses.
evaluated.reasoning: Increasing external financing at an increasing rate indicates that funding needs are compounding rather than stabilizing. Conditioning this acceleration on accumulated deficits distinguishes a rescue-financing spiral from a one-time capital raise for investment.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Loss-Making Rollover Without Deleveraging
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltis, dltr), at)), MUL(RANK(NEG(ABS(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ni, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: High gross debt-market activity predicts lower returns when it produces little change in the debt burden at loss-making firms.
evaluated.reasoning: Large issuance and repayment flows combined with an essentially unchanged debt ratio identify rollover churn directly, rather than applying the archived matched-flow template. The loss condition distinguishes necessary refinancing by distressed firms from routine maturity management by profitable borrowers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Debt-Heavy Funding Without Tax Capacity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltis, ADD(dltis, sstk))), RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(pi, at)), NEG(RATIO(txt, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Debt-heavy external financing predicts lower returns when firms lack taxable income and therefore receive little benefit from additional debt tax shields.
evaluated.reasoning: This compares debt with equity among active capital raisers instead of reversing the issuance-versus-repayment share from the prior signal. The negative sign aligns tax exhaustion with the added fixed-claim burden, avoiding a positive-return hypothesis that fights the adverse profitability exposure.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Operating Cash Debt-Service Coverage
evaluated.expression: RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(oancf, dltr), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms repaying debt, stronger operating cash flow relative to repayment obligations predicts higher returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This uses a conventional flow-to-flow coverage ratio and therefore avoids mixing the cash stock with annual financing flows. It also aligns the favorable debt-repayment effect with repayment capacity: low scores identify debt service unsupported by operations, while high scores identify sustainable deleveraging.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: External Payout Funding Shortfall
evaluated.expression: RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dvc, prstkc), oancf), ADD(dltis, sstk)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Returns are lower when the gap between shareholder payouts and operating cash flow is large relative to external capital raised.
evaluated.reasoning: This directly measures how much of an external financing round is associated with payouts unsupported by internal cash generation. Unlike the prior matched-flow template, the ratio distinguishes firms whose financing primarily covers a payout shortfall from those whose operations already support distributions.

evaluated.name: Debt Funding Under Cash-Flow Volatility
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltis, ADD(dltis, sstk))), RANK(VOL(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Debt-heavy external financing predicts lower returns when operating cash flow is unstable.
evaluated.reasoning: Volatile internal cash generation makes fixed debt claims particularly costly and raises the probability of future refinancing pressure. Comparing debt with equity among active capital raisers tests financing-source risk matching rather than the unconditional debt-issuance anomaly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Persistent Outflows Into Cash Decline
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(ADD(dltr, ADD(dvc, prstkc)), at), 3)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(oancf, at), 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Persistent debt repayments and shareholder distributions predict lower returns when operating cash flow is trending downward.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests temporal rigidity in financing outflows rather than another contemporaneous cash-coverage ratio. evaluated.name: Equity Substitution During Earnings Recovery
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(sstk, ADD(sstk, dltis)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(re, 1), LAG(at, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A shift toward equity financing predicts higher returns when retained earnings are recovering.
evaluated.reasoning: The financing leg measures a change in capital-source choice rather than a level share that is algebraically complementary to debt financing. evaluated.name: Lagged Capital Operating Payoff
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(LAG(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), at), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: External capital raised in the prior period predicts higher returns when it is followed by improving operating cash flow.
evaluated.reasoning: Lagging the financing event establishes a use-of-proceeds sequence and avoids dividing by negligible current issuance. The signal distinguishes productive capital raises that precede operating recovery from contemporaneous issuance associated with unresolved distress.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-Backed Payout Increase
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), at), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Increasing shareholder payouts predicts higher returns when operating cash flow is also improving.
evaluated.reasoning: The one-sided conjunction gives high scores only to payout increases supported by improving internal cash generation. Unlike the centered product, it does not treat payout cuts during cash-flow deterioration as a favorable state, eliminating the prior sign ambiguity.

evaluated.name: Debt-Funded Payout Deficit
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dvc, prstkc), oancf), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Long-term debt issuance predicts lower returns when shareholder payouts exceed operating cash flow.
evaluated.reasoning: The signal identifies firms adding fixed creditor claims while distributions to shareholders are unsupported by internal cash generation. evaluated.name: Cash-Supported Repayment Intensity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltr, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dltr), ADD(ABS(oancf), dltr))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Large debt repayments predict higher returns when operating cash flow is sufficient to absorb the repayment burden.
evaluated.reasoning: The bounded cash-surplus term remains well behaved when repayment is small and maps negative operating cash flow to an unambiguously adverse value. evaluated.name: Creditor Priority During Cash Recovery
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltr, ADD(dltr, ADD(dvc, prstkc)))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Prioritizing debt repayment over shareholder distributions predicts higher returns when operating cash flow is recovering.
evaluated.reasoning: The financing ratio measures creditor-versus-shareholder allocation among firms making cash outflows, not debt-versus-equity funding choice. evaluated.name: Equity Issuance After Liability Buildup
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sstk, at)), RANK(LAG(DELTA(RATIO(lct, at), 1), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity issuance predicts lower returns when it follows a prior increase in current liabilities.

evaluated.hypothesis: Equity issuance predicts higher returns when it reduces the debt burden after a prior accounting loss.

evaluated.name: Operating-Cash-Covered Payout

evaluated.hypothesis: Meaningful shareholder payouts predict higher returns when operating cash flow exceeds the distribution amount.

evaluated.name: Creditor-First Covered Payout
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, dltr), ADD(dvc, prstkc)), ADD(ABS(SUB(oancf, dltr)), ADD(dvc, prstkc)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Meaningful shareholder payouts predict higher returns when operating cash flow covers both debt repayment and the distribution.

evaluated.name: Successful Term-Out of Prior Liquidity Stress

considered.reasoning: Volatile internal cash generation makes fixed debt claims particularly costly and raises the probability of future refinancing pressure. Comparing debt with equity among active capital raisers tests financing-source risk matching rather than the unconditional debt-issuance anomaly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Persistent Outflows Into Cash Decline
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(ADD(dltr, ADD(dvc, prstkc)), at), 3)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(oancf, at), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: Persistent debt repayments and shareholder distributions predict lower returns when operating cash flow is trending downward.
considered.reasoning: This tests temporal rigidity in financing outflows rather than another contemporaneous cash-coverage ratio. Sustained distributions and repayments become hazardous when internal cash generation is deteriorating, while asset scaling avoids a near-zero financing-outflow denominator.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity Substitution During Earnings Recovery
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(sstk, ADD(sstk, dltis)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(re, 1), LAG(at, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A shift toward equity financing predicts higher returns when retained earnings are recovering.
considered.reasoning: The financing leg measures a change in capital-source choice rather than a level share that is algebraically complementary to debt financing. Retained-earnings improvement independently confirms operating recovery, so the signal is high only when recapitalization and recovery occur together.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Lagged Capital Operating Payoff
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(LAG(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), at), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: External capital raised in the prior period predicts higher returns when it is followed by improving operating cash flow.
considered.reasoning: Lagging the financing event establishes a use-of-proceeds sequence and avoids dividing by negligible current issuance. The signal distinguishes productive capital raises that precede operating recovery from contemporaneous issuance associated with unresolved distress.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-Backed Payout Increase
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), at), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Increasing shareholder payouts predicts higher returns when operating cash flow is also improving.
considered.reasoning: The one-sided conjunction gives high scores only to payout increases supported by improving internal cash generation. Unlike the centered product, it does not treat payout cuts during cash-flow deterioration as a favorable state, eliminating the prior sign ambiguity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt-Funded Payout Deficit
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dvc, prstkc), oancf), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Long-term debt issuance predicts lower returns when shareholder payouts exceed operating cash flow.
considered.reasoning: The signal identifies firms adding fixed creditor claims while distributions to shareholders are unsupported by internal cash generation. Scaling both components by assets avoids the small external-financing denominator in the prior payout-shortfall ratio and tests debt-funded payout pressure directly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-Supported Repayment Intensity
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltr, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dltr), ADD(ABS(oancf), dltr))))
considered.hypothesis: Large debt repayments predict higher returns when operating cash flow is sufficient to absorb the repayment burden.
considered.reasoning: The bounded cash-surplus term remains well behaved when repayment is small and maps negative operating cash flow to an unambiguously adverse value. Multiplying by repayment intensity ensures that high scores represent meaningful, internally supported debt reduction rather than profitable firms with negligible debt service.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Creditor Priority During Cash Recovery
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltr, ADD(dltr, ADD(dvc, prstkc)))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Prioritizing debt repayment over shareholder distributions predicts higher returns when operating cash flow is recovering.
considered.reasoning: The financing ratio measures creditor-versus-shareholder allocation among firms making cash outflows, not debt-versus-equity funding choice. Improving operating cash flow distinguishes prudent deleveraging during recovery from forced repayment by firms whose internal liquidity remains weak.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity Issuance After Liability Buildup
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sstk, at)), RANK(LAG(DELTA(RATIO(lct, at), 1), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Equity issuance predicts lower returns when it follows a prior increase in current liabilities.
considered.reasoning: The lagged liability change establishes that short-term pressure predates the equity raise, identifying last-resort financing rather than a contemporaneous accounting response. This sequencing mechanism differs from conditioning an equity funding share on another current-period recovery proxy.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Post-Loss Equity Debt Repair
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sstk, at)), MUL(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(LAG(RATIO(ni, at), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Equity issuance predicts higher returns when it reduces the debt burden after a prior accounting loss.
considered.reasoning: A lagged loss identifies the preexisting distress state, while the contemporaneous decline in debt-to-assets verifies that equity proceeds repair creditor claims. The signal therefore separates successful recapitalizations from loss-driven equity issuance that merely finances continued operations.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Operating-Cash-Covered Payout
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(dvc, prstkc)), ADD(ABS(oancf), ADD(dvc, prstkc)))))
considered.hypothesis: Meaningful shareholder payouts predict higher returns when operating cash flow exceeds the distribution amount.
considered.reasoning: The bounded surplus term distinguishes internally supported distributions from payouts made during cash deficits without using debt repayment as a misleading coverage denominator. Combining it with payout intensity prevents non-payers with positive cash flow from mechanically receiving the highest signal values.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Creditor-First Covered Payout
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, dltr), ADD(dvc, prstkc)), ADD(ABS(SUB(oancf, dltr)), ADD(dvc, prstkc)))))
considered.hypothesis: Meaningful shareholder payouts predict higher returns when operating cash flow covers both debt repayment and the distribution.
considered.reasoning: The bounded residual applies a creditor-first financing hierarchy: cash must cover debt service before a payout is considered sustainable. Payout intensity prevents non-distributing firms from dominating the favorable portfolio, while the bounded form avoids small payout denominators.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Successful Term-Out of Prior Liquidity Stress
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), MUL(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(lct, at), 1))), RANK(LAG(RATIO(SUB(lct, act), at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Long-term debt issuance predicts higher returns when it follows a working-capital deficit and accompanies a reduction in current liabilities.
considered.reasoning: The lagged funding deficit establishes preexisting liquidity stress, while the decline in current liabilities verifies that long-term proceeds term out short-term claims. This distinguishes successful maturity extension from the failed-refinancing signals whose portfolio alpha was negative.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Distressed Funding-Mix Instability
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(VOL(RATIO(SUB(dltis, sstk), at), 3)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Volatile switching between debt and equity financing predicts lower returns among firms with accumulated losses.
considered.reasoning: Volatility in the asset-scaled debt-minus-equity balance measures unstable funding-source access rather than the level of gross external financing. For deficit firms, repeated switching can reveal failed rescue rounds, market closure, or an inability to establish a durable capital structure.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Creditor Reprioritization During Cash Deterioration
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dltr, ADD(dltr, ADD(dvc, prstkc))), 1)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A shift from shareholder distributions toward debt repayment predicts lower returns when operating cash flow is deteriorating.
considered.reasoning: Increasing the creditor share of financing outflows during a cash-flow decline is more likely to reflect covenant pressure or forced amortization than voluntary balance-sheet repair. The signal uses changes in allocation and internal cash generation, avoiding another level external-financing or payout-shortfall construct.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity Resort After Debt-Access Retreat
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sstk, at)), MUL(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dltis, at), 1))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(lct, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Equity issuance predicts lower returns when debt issuance is retreating while current liabilities continue to rise.
considered.reasoning: The combination identifies firms resorting to equity as debt-market access weakens and short-term claims keep accumulating. This is a financing-sequence and market-access mechanism rather than another debt-and-equity co-issuance signal conditioned on cash flow.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Senior Dividend Burden Under Losses
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dvt, dvc), dvt)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ni, at))))
considered.hypothesis: A high preferred-dividend share predicts lower returns when the firm is loss-making.
considered.reasoning: The difference between total and common dividends proxies for senior preferred distributions, which are less flexible than common payouts and can intensify distress. Scaling by total dividends focuses on active payers and tests payout seniority rather than the unconditional dividend level.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Creditor-First Covered Dividend
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dvc, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, dltr), dvc), ADD(ABS(SUB(oancf, dltr)), dvc))))
considered.hypothesis: Common dividends predict higher returns when operating cash flow covers debt repayment before funding the dividend.
considered.reasoning: The bounded residual requires creditor obligations to be covered before treating the dividend as a resilience signal. Multiplying by dividend intensity prevents non-payers from receiving high scores and isolates whether durable common payouts drive the positive aggregate coverage result.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Creditor-First Covered Repurchase
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(prstkc, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, dltr), prstkc), ADD(ABS(SUB(oancf, dltr)), prstkc))))
considered.hypothesis: Share repurchases predict higher returns when operating cash flow covers debt repayment before funding the buyback.
considered.reasoning: Repurchases have favorable information content only when they do not compete with unsupported debt service. This controlled counterpart to the dividend signal tests whether the positive covered-payout effect is driven by flexible buybacks rather than recurring dividends.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt Issuance Under Service Shortfall
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltr, oancf), ADD(ABS(oancf), dltr))))
considered.hypothesis: Long-term debt issuance predicts lower returns when operating cash flow is insufficient relative to debt repayments.
considered.reasoning: The bounded shortfall term identifies genuinely uncovered debt service without dividing by a tiny repayment amount. New borrowing in that state is more likely to represent refinancing dependence than productive financing, aligning the issuance and distress channels in the negative direction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payout Into Deteriorating Debt Headroom
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dltr), ADD(ABS(oancf), dltr)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Shareholder payouts predict lower returns when operating cash headroom after debt service is deteriorating.
considered.reasoning: This tests failure to adjust payout policy to a worsening creditor-coverage trajectory, rather than another external-financing source for a contemporaneous payout deficit. The bounded headroom measure avoids division by small repayment values, while its change isolates deterioration rather than the level profitability effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Maturity Wall Under Cash-Flow Volatility
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltr, ADD(dltt, dlc))), RANK(VOL(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: Large debt repayments relative to outstanding debt predict lower returns when operating cash flow is unstable.
considered.reasoning: The repayment-to-debt ratio measures maturity concentration rather than debt issuance, net financing, or funding-source choice. A concentrated maturity wall is especially hazardous when volatile internal cash generation makes repayment capacity unreliable and refinancing more likely.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Failed Equity Risk Repair
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sstk, at)), MUL(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)), RANK(VOL(RATIO(oancf, at), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: Equity issuance predicts lower returns when the debt burden continues to rise at firms with volatile operating cash flow.
considered.reasoning: Meaningful equity issuance should reduce financing risk; rising debt-to-assets despite the raise demonstrates that the recapitalization failed to repair the balance sheet. Using issuance intensity avoids the degenerate equity-share ratio, while the negative sign aligns dilution, worsening debt burden, and cash-flow instability.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: Economically coherent conditional twist on the net-debt-issuance/external-financing anomaly, but the indicator zeroes out all non-burning firms so the spread partly compares "distressed high issuers" against an undifferentiated mass of zeros, and the incremental content beyond the known debt-issuance effect may be thin.

The expected positive sign bets against the well-documented negative debt-issuance/external-financing relation using *gross* dltis (which largely proxies for leverage and rollover intensity rather than net financing access), and the zero-masking of non-deficit firms makes the sorted spread hard to interpret if the sign does come out positive.

Conditioning on lt > at restricts the non-zero signal to the ~1-3% negative-book-equity tail, so the long portfolio will be tiny and unstable while the rest of the universe sits at exactly zero — a coverage/degeneracy problem that will dominate any economic content.

This is close to a direct rediscovery of the net share issuance anomaly combined with the already-published result that the issuance effect is concentrated among unprofitable/financially-constrained firms, so a negative slope would confirm known findings rather than reveal a new interaction.

Dividend-paying firms with an accumulated deficit are a genuinely interesting and under-studied conditioning cell and the smoothed payout ratio is sensibly constructed, though coverage of the non-zero cell will be small and part of any positive slope may simply reproduce the dividend-yield premium.

The MIN construction is creative but internally leaky — since dltr ≥ 0, MIN reduces to net equity issuance whenever that term is negative, so the short leg is populated by levered *repurchasers* rather than non-recapitalizers, which contradicts the stated mechanism and works against the buyback anomaly's known sign.

This is largely a permutation of two archived signals (net-debt-issuance × cash-burn indicator and MIN with a working-capital-deficit rank), swapping the liquidity proxy and MIN for MUL, and the rank-product form leaves the long leg economically mixed (low score can mean either low issuance or low burn), so the marginal information over the archive is thin.

The turnaround mechanism (repayment plus restored cash generation conditional on legacy losses) is coherent and sign-consistent, but the three-way MIN compresses dispersion and the long leg risks being a repackaged profitability/low-debt-issuance portfolio, so the incremental content over known anomalies is uncertain.

This is the archived Cash-Conversion Equity Dependence with one extra MIN conjunct bolted on—a cosmetic tightening rather than a diagnosis of why its FMB slope failed to translate into portfolio alpha—and the added low-cash term is itself a known cash-holdings anomaly leg.

The working-capital component's natural direction contradicts the stated expected sign, since a decline in working capital is low working-capital accruals, which the accrual anomaly associates with *higher* future returns; additionally, non-payers produce a large mass of exactly-zero dividend changes that will dominate the ranks.

Economically plausible, but the rank-product is likely dominated by the low-operating-cash-flow leg, making the short side a repackaged profitability anomaly rather than a test of repurchase quality, and the zero-mass of non-repurchasers in prstkc further muddies the ranking.

The failed-refinancing mechanism (gross long-term issuance that fails to retire growing short-term debt under a working-capital deficit) is a genuinely distinct maturity-structure story rather than a restatement of net debt issuance, though it overlaps the archived Liquidity-Strained Net Borrowing and the triple MIN will thin the extreme tail.

The expression is internally coherent (both ranks increase with the hypothesized state and the product is high exactly where returns are predicted high), and swapping the oancf level for its change plus dropping the deficit leg is a defensible response to the archive's dispersion-compressed three-way conjunction, though it remains close in spirit to the existing "Cash-Backed Distress Deleveraging" and its debt-repayment leg is largely the external-financing anomaly in reverse.

This is essentially the archive's "Failed Maturity Refinance" with the same three legs (long-term issuance, rising short-term debt, working-capital deficit) and the same sign, with DELTA(dlc) merely re-expressed as a 3-period TS_RANK — a cosmetic re-parameterization that additionally introduces a near-discrete, low-dispersion three-value ranking.

The mechanism (non-cash dilution via conversions/comp/discounted restructuring) is genuinely distinct from the standard net-share-issuance anomaly and the signal's direction matches the negative expected sign, but subtracting an assets-scaled cash-proceeds ratio from a share-count growth rate mixes incomparable units, so the composite will be dominated by whichever leg happens to have larger dispersion (ranking each leg before differencing would be cleaner).

The "failed recapitalization" test — issuance that fails to arrest rising liabilities at deficit firms — is an economically coherent and reasonably novel conditioning story with signs that match the expression, but it re-uses the same three-way MIN architecture whose dispersion compression the batch's own first proposal criticizes, so weak long-short spread magnitudes are the likely outcome.

The MIN of large repurchase spend and falling share count is close to a direct restatement of the published net-share-issuance/repurchase anomaly (Pontiff–Woodgate, Fama–French), which will dominate the composite, and the distress conditioning is likely to gut coverage since deficit firms rarely shrink share counts materially.

The second leg, (oancf − ib)/at, is simply negative total accruals, so the signal is a min-combination of dividend persistence with the Sloan accruals anomaly and any result will most plausibly be attributed to that known effect rather than to the claimed dividend cash-backing interaction.

Replacing the archive's issuance volatility with a signed deviation from the firm's own issuance norm is a genuine (if incremental) directional fix that plausibly restores cross-sectional sign consistency, and the multiplicative rank structure matches the stated negative expectation, though the underlying debt-issuance/liquidity mechanism is close to the well-known net-debt-issuance anomaly.

This is essentially a reparameterization of the archived "Debt-Demand Mismatch Spread" (net borrowing minus sales growth, both asset-scaled) with an industry rank wrapper, so it adds ranking cosmetics rather than a new mechanism, and it differences two economically incommensurate flows without addressing why the original slope was already only marginal.

The long leg is verbatim the archived "Recovery-Funded Net Repayment" (ls_talpha 0.57) and the short leg is verbatim the archived "Debt-Demand Mismatch" borrowing leg (ls_talpha -1.81), so this is a repackaging of two already-tested and individually weak constructs rather than a substantively different hypothesis.

The debt-for-equity-conversion mechanism is economically coherent and internally consistent with the positive expected sign, and the rank-differencing genuinely fixes the earlier unit mismatch, but the sign flip relative to "Unfunded Distress Dilution" looks partly data-motivated and the triple multiplicative rank interaction risks an unstable, effectively very narrow long tail.

Testing financing-source choice conditional on being an active capital raiser is a defensible sharpening of the equity-issuance/distress theme rather than a direct rediscovery, but the ratio is fragile when sstk and dltis are both near zero (and sstk is contaminated by option exercises), so coverage and tail stability need close scrutiny.

Swapping the earnings-volatility conditioner for cash accumulation is a substantive change with a clear "financing capacity confirms smoothing" rationale and a consistent positive sign, but the construct reduces to a two-way quality screen on dividend payers whose components (payout stability, change in cash holdings) are individually close to documented effects, and the dividend-history requirement keeps coverage thin.

This is a cosmetic re-specification of the archive's strongest signal, Dual-Market Distress Funding (same MIN-of-two-financing-legs × NEG(oancf) template with csho growth swapped for sstk and net for gross debt issuance), and its core leg duplicates the published net external financing / composite share issuance anomalies.

critic_notes.target_name: Record Debt Issuance Under Cash Gap
critic_notes.rationale: Replacing the 3-period moving average with a lagged 3-period maximum in Emergency Debt Issuance Spike is a mechanical variant of an already-tested signal, and since the earlier version's alpha came with a near-zero fmb_tstat (mirroring Episodic Debt Access Risk), the alpha almost certainly originates in the (lct−che)/at liquidity leg rather than in how issuance extremeness is measured.

The construction is internally coherent and correctly signed, but it is a near-cosmetic swap of the confirmation variable in the already-tested Recovery-Funded Net Repayment (Δoancf → −Δ(lct/act)), and Δ of a ratio-of-ratios is a noisy conditioner that is unlikely to rescue a leg (net debt retirement) whose standalone effect is the known debt-issuance anomaly.

The two legs are close to mechanically linked—raising equity (high sstk share) directly raises che—so a large part of the interaction is tautological rather than informative, and it recombines the equity-funding-share leg from Deficit Equity Funding Share with the Δ(che/at) leg from Cash-Rebuilding Dividend Stability without a new mechanism.

The shareholder-versus-creditor allocation ratio is a genuinely new construct in this archive with a coherent rollover-risk mechanism and a correctly signed interaction, though the denominator (dltr+dvc+prstkc) will be near zero for many firms, so coverage and tail stability should be checked.

The "financing churn" mechanism (matched payouts and external raises at cash-flow-weak firms) is economically distinct and well captured by the MIN operator, but it reuses the exact Dual-Market Distress Funding template and its payout leg pushes against the archive's evidence that payouts predict positive returns even among deficit firms, so the net sign is not assured.

This is a template clone of the archived "Dual-Market Distress Funding" (MIN of two financing flows scaled by assets, multiplied by RANK(NEG(oancf/at))) with only dltr substituted for sstk, so despite the plausible gross-rollover story it is a cosmetic variant rather than a substantively different mechanism.

Internally consistent (both legs are increasing in the "recovery" direction, matching the positive expected sign) and a genuine change-based reframing of the archived "Recovery-Funded Net Repayment," though it remains close to the well-known net-external-financing anomaly and its cash-flow-improvement leg overlaps with cash-flow/profitability momentum.

The repayment share dltr/(dltr+dltis) is by construction one minus the issuance share, so this is essentially a sign-flip of the archived "Tax-Exhausted Debt Issuance" combined with the same tax-capacity leg, and the low-pi/low-txt conditioning loads on unprofitable firms whose known negative return tilt (and FF5 RMW exposure) works against the stated positive sign.

The MIN(sstk, dltr) matched equity-for-debt recapitalization leg is a genuinely new construct relative to the archived "Equity-Funded Earnings Repair," but the conditioning leg is identical and DELTA(re)/lagged assets is close to a mechanical ROA-minus-payout measure, so much of the predictive content may simply be the profitability effect.

A one-term addition to the archived "Uncovered Debt Service Gap" that also introduces a sign conflict — the dominant dltr−dltis component is net debt repayment, which the literature and this archive ("Cash-Backed Distress Deleveraging," fmb 2.92) associate with *higher* returns, contradicting the stated negative expected sign — while mixing a cash stock with financing flows on the same scale.

The acceleration (second-difference) of gross external financing is a construct not yet used in the archive and the sign is coherent with both the external-financing anomaly and the distress conditioning, though the RANK(NEG(re/at)) conditioner is heavily reused and ACCEL on annual financing flows is likely noisy with reduced coverage.

This is a cosmetic denominator extension of the already-archived "Operating Cash Debt-Service Coverage" (adding dvc+prstkc to dltr), so it tests essentially the same cash-flow-to-outflow coverage mechanism with an additional near-zero-denominator instability rather than a substantively different economic idea.

The two poles use exactly complementary quantities (sstk/(sstk+dltis) = 1 − dltis/(sstk+dltis), and Δre vs NEG(Δre)), so min(r,s) − min(1−r,1−s) algebraically collapses to r+s−1 — a plain additive combination of equity-funding share and retained-earnings change with no conjunctive interaction at all, contradicting the stated design.

Scaling by gross issuance makes the score explode for firms with negligible capital raises, so the ratio largely proxies inverse issuance intensity (the well-known net-issuance anomaly) while the sales-growth numerator is signed against the documented negative growth/investment-return relation, leaving the expected positive sign poorly justified.

Economically coherent and sign-consistent (payouts unsupported by internal cash, scaled by the financing round), and a genuinely different functional form from the archived MIN-based "Externally Funded Distress Payout," though it overlaps that mechanism heavily and remains vulnerable to small-denominator noise despite winsorization.

The risk-matching mechanism is a substantively new conditioner for the debt-vs-equity funding share (unlike the archived tax-capacity version) and the multiplicative rank direction matches the negative expected sign, but the signal risks being dominated by the standalone cash-flow-volatility effect and should be checked against a volatility-only benchmark.

The product of two centered changes assigns equally high scores to payout increases with improving cash flow and to payout cuts with deteriorating cash flow — states with opposite documented return implications (dividend cuts predict low returns) — so the expression cannot represent the "alignment is good" hypothesis and its sign is ambiguous.

This is a cosmetic smoothing variant of the archive's already-tested "Operating Cash Debt-Service Coverage" (same ratio, same winsorization, same sign) and it does not address the deeper problem that oancf/dltr is non-monotonic when dltr is tiny or oancf negative, so a 3-year MA of both legs cannot be expected to deliver substantively new evidence.

The interaction of debt issuance intensity with an asset-scaled payout-minus-operating-cash gap is internally consistent (both legs increase in the direction of predicted underperformance) and the asset-scaling is a defensible fix to the unstable external-financing denominator of the earlier shortfall ratio, though the signal risks largely reloading the well-known net-external-financing anomaly through its dltis leg.

This is the third instance of the same template — RANK(dltis/(dltis+sstk)) multiplied by a distress conditioner — after the tax-capacity and cash-flow-volatility versions both failed, and swapping in the inverted coverage ratio is a conditioner substitution rather than a new mechanism, with the added problem that low oancf/dltr mostly identifies heavy repayers rather than genuinely uncovered firms.

This simply replaces the Δretained-earnings recovery proxy in the archive's "Equity-Funded Earnings Repair" with Δ(oancf/at), leaving the financing-share leg, functional form and expected sign unchanged — a cosmetic proxy swap rather than a substantively different hypothesis.

The first leg is identical to the archive's "Equity Substitution During Earnings Recovery" and only the conditioner changes, and the hypothesis's claim that current liabilities decline "subsequently" is not what the expression computes (DELTA(lct/at,1) is contemporaneous with the financing shift, so no forward-looking repair is tested).

Because low oancf/dltr is driven mainly by large dltr rather than by weak cash generation, the product of asset-scaled payouts and repayment intensity largely reconstructs the archive's "Financing Outflow Liquidity Burden" (dltr+dvc+prstkc scaled by a balance-sheet base), making this a near-rediscovery with a mislabeled "coverage" interpretation.

This is a cosmetic lag-plus-broadening variant of the archived "Debt-Funded Payout Deficit" (dltis × payout-minus-oancf, fmb −3.03, alpha −0.046) and closely overlaps "External Payout Funding Shortfall," and with annual data a one-year lag of a highly persistent payout-shortfall ratio adds little independent information.

Both multiplied terms are monotonically increasing in gross issuance, so the product is largely a rescaled restatement of the well-documented external-financing/net-issuance anomaly rather than a genuine cross-theme interaction, and it duplicates the archive's existing gross-financing-vs-cash-flow family.

Inserting debt service into the bounded payout-coverage residual is an economically motivated seniority refinement that combines two archive signals with partial support (payout coverage fmb 1.74; oancf/dltr fmb 2.30, alpha 0.040) and is internally consistent with the positive expected sign, though it remains an incremental extension rather than a new mechanism.

critic_notes.target_name: Successful Term-Out of Prior Liquidity Stress
critic_notes.rationale: The triple condition (issuance, falling current liabilities, prior working-capital deficit) is a coherent and internally consistent test of successful maturity extension that differs in construction from the archived "Failed Maturity Refinance" (lct rather than dlc, lagged deficit, positive sign), but it risks simply recovering the mirror image of that already-evaluated signal.

This is the archived "Dual-Market Distress Funding" (fmb −2.93, alpha −0.045, t −3.11) with a single one-year lag applied to a highly autocorrelated oancf/at term — a near-exact rediscovery whose economic content is essentially unchanged.

The net-debt-issuance × sales-contraction pairing is already the long leg of the archived "Debt-Demand Mismatch Spread" (fmb −1.94), and swapping MIN for MUL plus a one-year lag is an aggregator/timing tweak rather than a substantively different mechanism.

This is a single-token substitution (dltis → dltis−dltr) on the archive's already-tested "Debt-Funded Payout Deficit" with an identical mechanism and payout leg, i.e. exactly the cosmetic variant the objective discourages, and the net-issuance leg has already been probed repeatedly (Cash-Burn Debt Dependence, Liquidity-Strained Net Borrowing).

The expression is a straight mashup of two archived legs — MIN(dltis,sstk) from "Dual-Market Distress Funding" and the asset-scaled payout deficit from "Debt-Funded Payout Deficit" — and is economically near-identical to "Externally Funded Distress Payout," so it adds little independent information beyond the already-documented external-financing-plus-weak-cash-flow effect.

A legitimate attribution decomposition of the gen-8 "Creditor-First Covered Payout" (whose alpha was economically fine but statistically weak, t=1.36) with internally consistent construction and sign, though it is an incremental refinement rather than a new mechanism and partially overlaps the known dividend-payer/payout premium.

The repurchase counterpart is internally coherent and forms a useful paired test of which payout channel drives the covered-payout result, but prstkc/at is close to the published buyback-yield/net-share-issuance anomaly, so any positive result must be shown to survive beyond that known effect.

Sign and construction are consistent (high issuance × uncovered repayment → negative) and the bounded denominator sensibly fixes the scaling problem in the earlier "Uncovered Debt Service Gap"/"Cash-Supported Repayment Intensity" attempts, but dltis and dltr are mechanically correlated through rollover, so the signal risks collapsing into a gross debt-activity proxy.

The financing-mix ratio sstk/(sstk+dltis) is degenerate for near-zero issuers (a trivial equity raise with no debt issuance scores 1.0), and the signal is otherwise just the archived "Equity-Funded Earnings Repair" with the conditioner swapped, while the predicted positive sign for equity-heavy financing sits uncomfortably against the well-established equity-issuance underperformance without a clear argument for why coverage flips it.
